summary:
Maine is a comparatively low-risk state for a transgender visitor within the United States. A July 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment places Maine in its Low-Risk States group, while separately flagging that Maine's risk has increased because the University of Maine system capitulated to federal restrictions on trans sports participation.

The University of Maine System announced compliance with federal restrictions on transgender sports participation on 21 March 2025 (updated 24 March), following suspension by the US Department of Agriculture of federal funding for research and programs while it investigated possible sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programmes.

Maine law prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity or expression in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and education opportunity. The protection was added in 2005 and retained after a November 8, 2005 veto referendum; LD1688, signed 17 June 2021, explicitly extends gender identity throughout state statutes. Maine's hate crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity. The gay and trans panic defense was banned by legislation passed in June 2019 (House 132-1, Senate 35-0), effective 1 July 2019.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since November 2019 no medical provider certification is required to change the gender marker on driver's licences and state IDs; a completed Gender Designation Form with male, female and X options suffices. Birth certificates reflecting gender identity, including X, have been available since July 2020 upon notarized affidavit, though X requires a declaration from a licensed physician or mental health provider and minors require parental consent.

Facilities access is protected. In January 2014 the Maine Supreme Court ruled in Doe v. Regional School Unit 26 against a district that denied a student bathroom use aligned with gender identity. Beginning 1 October 2026, healthcare facilities must mandate and include sexual orientation and gender identity data.

Gender-affirming care is protected rather than banned. A law effective since July 2023 allows 16 and 17 year olds to access hormone therapy for gender-affirming healthcare, and an April 2024 law explicitly protects, defends and safeguards gender-affirming healthcare. A bill that would have provided sanctuary protections to trans minors was unanimously struck down by Maine Democrats in January 2024 following backlash.

On sports, in June 2025 the Maine Senate rejected Legislative Document 233, which would have prohibited transgender women from competing in women's sports in state-funded schools; it was the only one of eight anti-trans bills in 2025 to pass the House.

Correctional placement is documented. Andrea Balcer, a 27-year-old transgender woman and convicted double murderer, is housed in the women's facility at the Maine Correctional Center in Windham, where she has been held for at least a year as of April 2026, meaning placement by current gender identity rather than birth sex. On 3 April 2026 inmate Katie Mountain (41) filed a 30-page complaint against MDOC Commissioner Randall Liberty, Warden Ben Beal and Balcer, alleging chronic harassment and assault by the trans prisoner; attorney Cynthia Dill filed it. No ruling has been reported. The harassment and assault claims are allegations, while the placement of a trans woman in the women's prison is documented.
tangentialFactors:
Maine repealed criminalization of same-sex sexual activity in 1976, legalizing sodomy between heterosexual partners at the same time, with age of consent set at 16. Maine law prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived sexual orientation in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and education opportunity, added in 2005 and retained after voters defeated a veto referendum on November 8, 2005. Maine's hate crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived sexual orientation. Licensed health care providers are prohibited from practicing conversion therapy on minors under legislation signed 29 May 2019 and effective 17 September 2019.

The Maine Human Rights Act, 5 M.R.S. §4551 et seq., was amended by PL 2005, c. 10 (LD 1196) to extend civil-rights protections regardless of sexual orientation, following repeal of the 1997 protections (PL 1997, c. 205) in the February 10, 1998 people's veto and defeat of the 1999 protections (PL 1999, c. 629) in the November 7, 2000 referendum; the 2005 protections survived the November 8, 2005 people's veto referendum.
localsOnly:
Residents benefit from the full stack of state protections: gender identity discrimination bans across employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and education; hate-crime penalty enhancements for gender identity; a ban on the gay and trans panic defense since July 2019; open gender-marker change on licences and birth certificates including X; constitutional bathroom access since Doe v. Regional School Unit 26 (2014); statutory protection of gender-affirming care since April 2024 with hormone therapy accessible to 16 and 17 year olds since July 2023; and a conversion therapy ban on minors since September 2019.

From 1 October 2026 healthcare facilities in Maine must mandate and include sexual orientation and gender identity data.

Transgender women incarcerated in state facilities are housed according to current gender identity; the placement of Andrea Balcer in the Maine Correctional Center women's facility is the documented instance, with litigation pending and no ruling reported.
outOfScopeNotes:
The July 2026 assessment's flag that Maine's risk has increased due to University of Maine System capitulation on sports restrictions is stated as the assessment's finding; the operational effect of that compliance on students or visitors is not sourced here.

The harassment and assault allegations in the Mountain v. Liberty complaint are unadjudicated; no ruling has been reported as of the source date.

The federal layer governing a trans visitor in Maine (passport markers, entry screening, federal facility rules) is carried by the national record and is not restated here.
